intro.title: Ramadan Prep: 30 Days to Get Ready
intro.body: Ramadan is coming, and a beautiful way to welcome it is to arrive ready. Over the next 30 days you will steady your salah, build a daily bond with the Quran, and prepare your body, heart and home, one small step at a time. Go gently, keep going, and make every step for Allah.

tracks.name: Salah
tracks.desc: All five on time, Fajr, careful wudu, understanding what you recite, and Sunnah prayers

tracks.name: Quran
tracks.desc: A fixed daily Quran time, growing toward about 20 pages a day, with understanding

tracks.name: Fasting
tracks.desc: Sunnah fasts, making up missed days, and planning suhoor and iftar

tracks.name: Heart
tracks.desc: Tawbah, sincere intentions, dua, and mending ties with family and friends

tracks.name: Habits
tracks.desc: Sleep, food, caffeine and screen time shaped to support your worship

tracks.name: Charity
tracks.desc: Regular giving, a Ramadan charity plan, and zakat al-fitr ready on time

assessment.q: How many of the five daily prayers do you usually pray on time?
How often do you pray Fajr on time?
How often do you read the Quran at the moment?
How comfortable are you reading the Quran in the Arabic script?
options: I read slowly, letter by letter
I read fairly well, with some mistakes

assessment.q: Do you have missed Ramadan fasts still to make up?
options: Yes, and I am not sure how many
Yes, I know how many but have no plan yet
Yes, and I have dates planned

assessment.q: How would you describe your sleep and screen habits most nights?
options: Late nights and lots of scrolling
Often late, with screens before bed
Mostly regular, with a few late nights
Regular sleep and screens under control

assessment.q: How often do you give charity?
options: Mainly in Ramadan or on special occasions

days.reflect: Which prayer is hardest for me to pray on time, and what usually gets in the way?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ was asked which deed Allah loves most. He said: prayer offered at its proper time.

prompts.text: Look up today's five prayer times and set an alert a little before each one.
prompts.tip: Use a prayer-times app or your mosque's timetable. An early alert gives you time to finish what you are doing and make wudu.

prompts.text: Pray all five prayers within their times today, ticking each one off as you go.
prompts.tip: Notice which prayer is hardest to catch. That is the one to plan around this week, not a reason to feel bad.

prompts.text: Make a sincere intention that these 30 days are for Allah, and write down why you want to prepare.
prompts.tip: Keep it short and honest, e.g. 'I want to meet Ramadan ready and close to Allah.' Read it again whenever your energy dips.

days.theme: Fajr: start the day with Allah
days.reflect: How did praying Fajr on time feel, or what would help me catch it tomorrow?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Whoever prays Fajr is under the protection of Allah.

prompts.text: Set two alarms for Fajr and put one across the room, so you have to get up to turn it off.
prompts.tip: Make wudu as soon as you are up; the cool water helps you wake. If you oversleep, do not give up: pray it and try again.

prompts.text: Go to bed a little earlier tonight so that waking for Fajr feels easier.
prompts.tip: Count back from Fajr time to find a bedtime that gives you enough sleep, and start winding down half an hour before it.

prompts.text: Ask a family member or friend to be your Fajr partner, checking on each other each morning.
prompts.tip: Agree on a quick message after the adhan. Encouraging each other makes hard mornings far easier to get through.

days.reflect: How did taking care over wudu change the way I began my prayers today?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Whoever performs wudu and does it well, his sins leave his body, even from beneath his nails.

prompts.text: Make each wudu today slowly and completely, washing every part fully and in order.
prompts.tip: Go slowly but use water sparingly: the Prophet ﷺ made wudu with one mudd, a small amount of water (Bukhari 201).

prompts.text: Learn the dua after wudu and say it each time you finish today.
prompts.tip: Ashhadu an la ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh (Muslim 234).

prompts.text: Plan how you will make wudu at work, school or when out, so it never makes you late.
prompts.tip: Find the nearest washroom or prayer room in advance. Some people make wudu before leaving home and try to keep it.

days.reflect: Which ayah of Al-Fatiha touched me most today, and why?
days.mot: Allah said: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant. When he says 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds', Allah says: My servant has praised Me.

prompts.text: Read a simple translation of Al-Fatiha, one ayah at a time, until you know what each line means.
prompts.tip: Write each ayah's meaning on a small card and keep it by your prayer mat. Read it before you pray today.

prompts.text: In at least one prayer today, recite Al-Fatiha slowly, thinking about each ayah as you say it.
prompts.tip: Pause briefly at the end of each ayah. Slowing down a little lets your heart catch up with your tongue.

prompts.text: Reflect on the dua in Al-Fatiha, 'Guide us to the straight path', and the guidance you most need.
prompts.tip: Allah says of Al-Fatiha's last ayat: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked (Muslim 395).

days.theme: The words of ruku and sujood
days.reflect: Which words of my prayer do I now understand that I used to say without thinking?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: The nearest a servant is to his Lord is when he is in sujood, so make plenty of dua then.

prompts.text: Learn the meaning of what you say in ruku and sujood, and think of it as you pray today.
prompts.tip: Subhana Rabbiyal 'Adhim: Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great. Subhana Rabbiyal A'la: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.

prompts.text: Learn the meaning of the tashahhud (at-tahiyyat) that you recite while sitting.
prompts.tip: Read it line by line with a translation: greetings to Allah, peace on the Prophet ﷺ and the righteous, then the testimony of faith.

prompts.text: Learn the sujood dua 'O Allah, forgive me all my sins' in Arabic, and say it in your sujood today.
prompts.tip: Allahummaghfir li dhanbi kullahu, diqqahu wa jillahu, wa awwalahu wa akhirahu, wa 'alaniyatahu wa sirrahu (Muslim 483).

days.reflect: Which Sunnah prayer can I make a lifelong habit, starting this week?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Whoever prays twelve voluntary rak'ahs each day for Allah, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise.

prompts.text: Pray the two short Sunnah rak'ahs before Fajr today, if you do not already.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ said the two rak'ahs before Fajr are better than this world and all it contains (Muslim 725).

prompts.text: Add one more Sunnah prayer to your day, such as the two rak'ahs after Maghrib.
prompts.tip: Build toward the twelve: 2 before Fajr, 4 before Dhuhr, 2 after Dhuhr, 2 after Maghrib and 2 after Isha (Tirmidhi 415).

prompts.text: Pray witr before you sleep tonight, so your night ends with prayer.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ advised Abu Hurayrah to pray witr before sleeping (Bukhari 1981), a good habit if waking at night is hard.

days.reflect: Looking back on this week, which salah habit grew most, and which needs more care?
days.mot: Successful indeed are the believers: those who are humble and attentive in their prayer.

prompts.text: Pray each prayer today without rushing, letting each position settle before you move on.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ taught a man who prayed hastily to bow, prostrate and sit until he was at ease in each (Bukhari 757).

prompts.text: Before each prayer today, take a few seconds to silence your phone and clear your mind.
prompts.tip: Face the qiblah, breathe, and remember who you are standing before. A short pause before Allahu Akbar helps focus.

prompts.text: Plan one or two voluntary fasts for the coming week, such as a Monday or Thursday.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ used to try to fast on Mondays and Thursdays (Tirmidhi 745). Starting gently now makes Ramadan's first days easier.

days.reflect: What time of day suits me best for the Quran, and what might get in its way?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Read the Quran, for on the Day of Resurrection it will come as an intercessor for its companions.

prompts.text: Choose one fixed daily time for the Quran, such as after Fajr, and read 2 pages in it today.
prompts.tip: Tie it to something you already do, like a prayer. If you cannot read Arabic yet, listen while following a translation.

prompts.text: Put your mushaf or Quran app where you will see it at your chosen time.
prompts.tip: Move distracting apps off your phone's home screen and put the Quran app there. A bookmark saves time finding your page.

prompts.text: Keep praying all five on time, and keep one Sunnah prayer from last week going.
prompts.tip: Tick your prayers off each day so last week's gains are not lost while your focus moves to the Quran.

days.reflect: What page goal can I truly keep every day, even on busy days?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: The most beloved deed to Allah is the one done regularly, even if it is small.

prompts.text: Write your page goals: about 5 a day by day 14, 10 a day by day 21 and 20 a day by day 29.
prompts.tip: About 20 pages a day completes the Quran in a 30-day Ramadan. If that is too much for now, choose smaller steps you can keep.

prompts.text: Read 3 pages today in your fixed Quran time.
prompts.tip: Each letter you read brings a good deed, multiplied by ten (Tirmidhi 2910). Short daily reading builds the stamina Ramadan needs.

prompts.text: If you have Ramadan fasts to make up, count them today so there is time to fit them in.
prompts.tip: Allah says whoever was ill or travelling makes up an equal number of other days (Quran 2:184). Starting early leaves room.

days.reflect: Which recitation mistake will I work on first, and who can help me with it?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: The one skilled in the Quran is with the noble, righteous angels, and the one who stumbles over it, finding it hard, has two rewards.

prompts.text: Find a Quran teacher, class or recitation app that can check your reading regularly.
prompts.tip: Ask your mosque about Quran classes, or use an app that listens and corrects. Work on one or two rules at a time.

prompts.text: Listen to a skilled reciter read today's pages before you read them yourself.
prompts.tip: Follow the text with your eyes or finger as you listen, then read it yourself, copying the pronunciation and pace.

prompts.text: Recite the surahs you use in salah to someone who can check your pronunciation.
prompts.tip: Start with Al-Fatiha, the heart of every prayer. Small corrections here improve every prayer you pray.

days.reflect: What is Allah telling me in the surah I studied today, and how will I live it?
days.mot: A blessed Book which We have revealed to you, so that they may reflect upon its verses and people of understanding may take heed.

prompts.text: Read a simple tafsir of one short surah, such as Al-'Asr or Al-Kawthar.
prompts.tip: Use a trusted tafsir in your language. Read the surah, then its explanation, then the surah again with fresh eyes.

prompts.text: Write down one lesson from that surah and one way you will act on it this week.
prompts.tip: Keep a small Quran journal. One line is enough: what Allah is saying, and one thing you will change because of it.

prompts.text: Recite that surah in one of your prayers today with its meaning in mind.
prompts.tip: Reciting what you understand helps your heart stay present. If you do not know it by heart yet, use a surah you do know.

days.reflect: Which ayat do I want to carry in my heart this Ramadan, and why?
days.mot: And We have certainly made the Quran easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?

prompts.text: Memorise one to three new ayat today, repeating each until you can say it without looking.
prompts.tip: Listen to the ayat first, then repeat each one many times before joining them. Revise them after each prayer today.

prompts.text: Recite the ayat you memorised today in one of your prayers.
prompts.tip: Using new ayat in salah helps them stick. If you feel unsure, read them over once more just before you pray.

prompts.text: Teach a child or friend one short surah, or the meaning of one you know.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ said the best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it (Bukhari 5027).

days.reflect: Which surah I once knew has slipped away, and how can I bring it back?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Keep revising the Quran, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it slips away faster than a camel from its rope.

prompts.text: Revise the surahs you already know by reciting them from memory, slowly and carefully.
prompts.tip: Recite to a family member or into a voice note, then check it against the mushaf. Mark any spots that need more work.

prompts.text: Read 5 pages today in your fixed Quran time.
prompts.tip: If this feels like a jump, split it: some pages after Fajr and the rest after another prayer.

prompts.text: Start a small daily charity habit: set aside a coin or a small amount each day until Ramadan.
prompts.tip: Use a jar at home or a donation app. Regular giving, even a little, builds a habit you will carry into Ramadan.

days.reflect: Where will the Quran fit in my Ramadan day, and what will I move to make room for it?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ told Abdullah ibn Amr: Recite the whole Quran in one month.

prompts.text: Make your Ramadan reading plan: how many pages a day, and at which times.
prompts.tip: One juz a day completes the Quran in 30 days. In the 604-page Madinah mushaf that is about 20 pages, or 4 after each prayer.

prompts.text: Ask a friend or family member to be your Quran partner in Ramadan, to read with or check in with.
prompts.tip: Each night of Ramadan Jibreel met the Prophet ﷺ, who recited the Quran to him (Bukhari 1902). A partner helps on tired days.

prompts.text: Support Quran learning: give to a Quran class or school, or gift someone a translation.
prompts.tip: Ask your mosque or a local Quran school what they need. A mushaf with translation can be a lasting gift for a new reader.

days.reflect: What do I hope fasting before Ramadan will teach me about myself?
days.mot: Aisha said: I never saw the Prophet ﷺ fast a whole month except Ramadan, nor fast more in any month than in Sha'ban.

prompts.text: Check your fasting plan for late Sha'ban: scholars differ on starting new voluntary fasts after mid-Sha'ban.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ said not to fast a day or two before Ramadan unless it is a fast you usually keep (Bukhari 1914). Unsure? Ask a local scholar.

prompts.text: On your next fast day, note how your body and mood cope, to guide your Ramadan plans.
prompts.tip: Jot down energy dips, hunger times or headaches. These notes will shape your suhoor, iftar and sleep plans this week.

prompts.text: Read 6 pages today in your fixed Quran time.
prompts.tip: If you are fasting, the quiet hour before iftar is a lovely time to read and make dua.

days.reflect: What helps me keep commitments to Allah that no one else sees?
days.mot: Aisha said: I would have Ramadan fasts to make up, and I could only make them up in Sha'ban.

prompts.text: If you owe any fasts, book a date for each one before Ramadan and put them in your calendar.
prompts.tip: Spread them out if that is easier. If you are unsure what you owe or how to make it up, ask a trusted local scholar.

prompts.text: Support anyone at home who is making up fasts: wake them for suhoor or help prepare their iftar.
prompts.tip: Many people have days to make up. Ask what would help, then do it quietly and kindly.

prompts.text: After each of the five prayers today, say SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah and Allahu Akbar 33 times each.
prompts.tip: Complete 100 with 'La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamdu wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir' (Muslim 597).

days.reflect: What keeps me up late, and what am I willing to let go of to sleep earlier?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ told Abdullah ibn Amr: Pray at night and also sleep, for your body has a right over you.

prompts.text: Choose a regular bedtime that gives you enough sleep before Fajr, and start it tonight.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ disliked sleeping before Isha and chatting after it (Bukhari 568). Count back from Fajr to set your bedtime.

prompts.text: Try the Sunnah bedtime routine tonight: wudu, lie on your right side and say the bedtime dua.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ taught al-Bara this routine with a dua beginning 'Allahumma aslamtu wajhi ilayk' (Bukhari 6311).

prompts.text: Pray Isha on time tonight, then keep the rest of the evening calm so you can sleep early.
prompts.tip: Dim the lights, put screens away and lay out what you need for the morning. A calm evening makes Fajr easier.

days.reflect: What would a calm, unhurried suhoor look like in my home?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Eat suhoor, for there is blessing in suhoor.

prompts.text: Plan three or four simple suhoor meals you can rotate through Ramadan.
prompts.tip: Choose foods that keep you going, such as oats, eggs, yoghurt, dates and fruit, with plenty of water. Prep the night before.

prompts.text: On your next fast day, wake early enough to eat suhoor calmly before Fajr.
prompts.tip: Eating close to Fajr follows the Sunnah: the gap between the Prophet's suhoor and the adhan was about fifty ayat (Bukhari 1921).

prompts.text: Read 8 pages today in your fixed Quran time.
prompts.tip: Try reading part of it in the quiet time after suhoor or Fajr, when the house is still and the mind is fresh.

days.reflect: How can my iftar table become a place of gratitude and sharing, not just eating?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ would break his fast before praying with fresh dates; if there were none, dried dates; and if none, a few sips of water.

prompts.text: Plan iftars that begin simply with dates and water, followed later by a moderate meal.
prompts.tip: Keep dates and water ready before sunset so you can break your fast on time. Batch-cook a few meals ahead to save time.

prompts.text: Plan how you will pray Maghrib on time after breaking your fast, at home or at the mosque.
prompts.tip: Break the fast lightly, pray, then sit down to eat. Agree this routine with your household so no one feels rushed.

prompts.text: Choose a night in Ramadan to share iftar with a neighbour, a relative or your local mosque.
prompts.tip: Whoever gives a fasting person food to break their fast gets the same reward, without reducing theirs (Tirmidhi 807).

days.reflect: Which food or drink habit has a hold on me, and how will I loosen it before Ramadan?
days.mot: O children of Adam... eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.

prompts.text: If you drink tea or coffee, have one cup less today and keep easing off until Ramadan.
prompts.tip: Swap that cup for water or a caffeine-free drink. Cutting down slowly now can make the first days of fasting easier.

prompts.text: Swap one sugary snack or drink today for fruit, dates, nuts or water.
prompts.tip: Notice when you reach for sugar out of habit or boredom, and keep a better option in your bag or kitchen.

prompts.text: Read 9 pages today, using an old coffee or snack break for some of them.
prompts.tip: Replacing a habit with a better one is easier than just stopping. Keep your mushaf or Quran app near your usual break spot.

days.reflect: What do I want fasting to change in me this Ramadan, beyond going without food?
days.mot: O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become righteous.

prompts.text: Draft your Ramadan daily timetable from suhoor to sleep, built around the fast and the five prayers.
prompts.tip: Block out suhoor, prayers, Quran, work or school, a rest, iftar and night prayer. Leave some gaps; a realistic plan lasts.

prompts.text: Decide where you will pray the night prayers of Ramadan, and check your mosque's timings.
prompts.tip: If you will pray at home, set up a space and choose what you will recite. A plan made now is easier to keep.

prompts.text: Read 10 pages today: try 2 pages after each of the five prayers.
prompts.tip: That is half a Ramadan day's reading. Notice how it fits around your prayers; next week you will build on it.

days.reflect: How does Allah's promise of mercy change the way I see my mistakes, and what will I change?
days.mot: Say: O My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.

prompts.text: Sit alone for a few minutes, think of the sins you want to leave, and sincerely ask Allah to forgive you.
prompts.tip: Tawbah means stopping the sin, regretting it, resolving not to return, and putting right any wrong done to others.

prompts.text: Choose one habit you want to leave before Ramadan and take one step away from it today.
prompts.tip: Remove the trigger: delete the app, avoid the place, or tell a trusted friend. Put something good in its place.

prompts.text: Pray two rak'ahs today, then sincerely ask Allah for forgiveness.
prompts.tip: Whoever sins, then makes wudu well, prays two rak'ahs and asks Allah's forgiveness, Allah forgives him (Abu Dawud 1521).

days.reflect: Why do I really want this Ramadan to be different, and who am I doing it for?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: Whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, Allah records one full good deed; if he does it, ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times or more.

prompts.text: Write three intentions for Ramadan, for Allah's sake: one for worship, one for character, one for others.
prompts.tip: Be specific, e.g. 'pray Fajr on time', 'control my anger', 'call my aunt weekly'. Keep the list where you will see it daily.

prompts.text: Before each good deed today, pause and renew your intention to do it for Allah alone.
prompts.tip: A quick inner reminder is enough: 'This is for You, O Allah.' Work, study and cooking can be done with that intention too.

prompts.text: Read 12 pages today, renewing your intention before you open the mushaf.
prompts.tip: Read to be guided, not only to finish. Pause at one ayah that speaks to you and note it down.

days.reflect: If I could ask Allah for only three things this Ramadan, what would they be?
days.mot: When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me.

prompts.text: Start your Ramadan dua list: what you want to ask Allah for, for yourself and for others.
prompts.tip: Include this life and the next, family, friends, the sick and the wider Ummah. Keep it on your phone so it is always with you.

prompts.text: Make dua from your list after one of your prayers today, asking with full hope.
prompts.tip: Add duas from the Quran and Sunnah too. The Prophet's most frequent dua was 'Allahumma rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah...' (Bukhari 6389).

prompts.text: Ask a family member or friend what they would like you to pray for, and add it to your list.
prompts.tip: When you pray for a fellow Muslim in their absence, the angel appointed to you says: 'Amin, and for you the same' (Muslim 2732).

days.reflect: Whose relationship with me needs mending, and what small step can I take this week?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: The one who truly keeps family ties is not the one who returns kindness, but the one who reconnects when ties are cut.

prompts.text: Reach out to one relative or friend you have drifted from, with a kind message or a call.
prompts.tip: Keep it simple: a salam, a dua or asking after their health. You do not need to fix everything at once; just open the door.

prompts.text: Apologise to someone you have wronged, or quietly forgive someone who wronged you.
prompts.tip: If a relationship is not safe, you can keep a healthy distance and still make dua for them. Forgiveness starts in the heart.

prompts.text: Read 15 pages today; if time is short, listen to some of them while travelling or cooking.
prompts.tip: Listening keeps you connected on busy days. Follow along in the mushaf when you can, so your eyes learn the pages too.

days.reflect: How can I make giving a joyful daily habit rather than a once-a-year duty?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ made zakat al-fitr a purification for the fasting person from idle and indecent talk, and food for the poor.

prompts.text: Set your Ramadan charity budget and choose the causes you will support.
prompts.tip: Split it across the month so you give something every day. Think of local needs, relatives in need and trusted charities.

prompts.text: Find out your mosque's zakat al-fitr amount and deadline, and note it for each person you pay it for.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ made it due on every Muslim, young or old, and ordered it paid before the Eid prayer (Bukhari 1503).

prompts.text: Check this week's prayers and fix the one that most often slips past its time.
prompts.tip: Look at what got in the way and make one small change, like an earlier alarm or a reminder before you leave work.

days.reflect: What do I want my family to remember about this Ramadan in years to come?
days.mot: And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it.

prompts.text: Hold a short family or household meeting to share Ramadan goals and share out the chores.
prompts.tip: Let everyone, even young children, choose one goal. Shared chores mean everyone gets time to pray, read and rest.

prompts.text: Agree on one prayer each day in Ramadan that your household will pray together.
prompts.tip: Maghrib after iftar or Isha before bed often suits families. Let children take turns choosing a dua to say afterwards.

prompts.text: Set up a family charity jar that everyone, including the children, adds to during Ramadan.
prompts.tip: Agree together where it will go, and let the children help hand it over so they see the good it does.

days.reflect: What would I need to change in my routine to give the last ten nights my very best?
days.mot: Aisha said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ strove in worship in the last ten nights more than at any other time.

prompts.text: Plan your night prayers for the last ten nights: where you will pray, when and for how long.
prompts.tip: Lighten those days if you can: book time off, cook ahead and agree family routines, so the nights get your best.

prompts.text: Choose a few duas to repeat in the last ten nights, and add them to your dua list.
prompts.tip: In the last third of every night Allah says: Who is calling on Me, that I may answer him? (Bukhari 1145).

prompts.text: Mark the last ten nights in your calendar, highlighting the odd ones, as nights to give your best.
prompts.tip: The Prophet ﷺ said to seek Laylatul Qadr in the odd nights of the last ten (Bukhari 2017). Confirm the dates once Ramadan begins.

days.reflect: How many hours did screens take from me last week, and what could those hours become in Ramadan?
days.mot: The Prophet ﷺ said: There are two blessings that many people lose out on: good health and free time.

prompts.text: Check your screen-time report and set a daily limit for Ramadan.
prompts.tip: Most phones show daily use in settings. Set app limits, mute busy group chats and turn off notifications you do not need.

prompts.text: Choose screen-free times for Ramadan, such as suhoor, the hour before iftar and the night prayers.
prompts.tip: Charge your phone outside the bedroom and use a simple alarm clock. Let friends know you will reply less in Ramadan.

prompts.text: Read 20 pages today as a test run: 4 pages after each of the five prayers.
prompts.tip: If you do not finish, note how far you got. That is your honest starting point, and you can build from there.

days.reflect: Looking back on these 30 days, what has changed in me, and what will I carry into Ramadan?
days.mot: The month of Ramadan is the one in which the Quran was revealed as guidance for people... Allah intends ease for you, not hardship.

prompts.text: Choose the one salah habit you will guard most closely in Ramadan, and write it down.
prompts.tip: Look back at week one: on time, Fajr, wudu, meaning, Sunnah prayers and focus. Pick one and ask Allah to help you with it.

prompts.text: Set out your mushaf, bookmark and page plan so you can start reading on the first day.
prompts.tip: Keep the mushaf where you pray and write your daily target on your bookmark. Begin on day one, even if just a few pages.

prompts.text: Read your intentions and dua list again, and ask Allah to help you make the most of Ramadan.
prompts.tip: Check your suhoor food, iftar plan, bedtime, charity plan and screen limits too. Then rest: you have prepared well.

milestones.title: Salah foundations
milestones.goal: Pray all five on time, guard Fajr, make wudu with care, understand what you recite and add the Sunnah prayers.

milestones.title: Quran connection
milestones.goal: Keep a fixed daily Quran time, grow to about 5 pages a day, check your recitation and understand a short surah.

milestones.title: Fasting and body
milestones.goal: Follow the Sunnah in your fasts, book any make-up days, reset your sleep, plan suhoor and iftar, and ease off caffeine and sugar.

milestones.title: Heart and community
milestones.goal: Turn to Allah, set intentions, write a dua list, mend ties, plan charity and the last ten nights, and build up to about 20 pages a day.
